Configure your server

Tools and integrations

Configure the services bots reach beyond the model: web search, memory, MCP servers, apps, messaging, cloud coding agents and payments.

Web search and page reading

Builtin web_search and web_fetch use keyless HTTP search (DuckDuckGo HTML) and local Readability extraction by default. To choose Parallel Search MCP, set WEB_PROVIDER=parallel in .env and restart both the API and worker. The same bot tools then return search excerpts and extracted page markdown through HTTPS MCP at https://search.parallel.ai/mcp. Search uses Fast mode without an account or API key.

This option sends search queries and requested page URLs to Parallel, which retrieves pages on its servers. Conversation accounting uses an HMAC of internal IDs keyed by ENCRYPTION_KEY (shared by the API and worker), so deployments with distinct secrets send distinct session IDs. Rotating that secret resets the session IDs; the existing development-only encryption-key fallback also applies here. Anonymous access has service limits; rate-limit and provider errors are returned to the bot without switching providers. Per-bot disabled web tools remain disabled. Set WEB_PROVIDER=keyless-http (or remove the setting) to return to the default.

To choose Keenable instead, set WEB_PROVIDER=keenable and restart both the API and worker. The same bot tools then return search snippets and extracted page markdown through HTTPS MCP at https://api.keenable.ai/mcp, without an account or API key. This option sends search queries and requested page URLs to Keenable, which retrieves pages on its servers. Anonymous access is rate limited per IP address; set KEENABLE_API_KEY on the API and worker to send a key and lift those limits. Errors, per-bot disabled tools and the way back to the default work as described for Parallel.

Self-hosted memory

Supermemory and Honcho can run on your own network. In Settings → Memory, choose Local and enter the instance’s base URL. The operator must set MCP_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINT=true; workspace owners can then save a local endpoint. It must be loopback or resolve to private addresses (a Compose service name, an RFC1918 or unique-local address, or a .internal name such as Railway’s private network); WhatEverFi pins the resolved address for every request. Space members use the saved connection without seeing its key.

For Honcho, enable AUTH_USE_AUTH on the Honcho server and use an admin JWT from its scripts/generate_jwt.py --admin as the key, so each Space gets its own workspace. A workspace-scoped JWT works when you enter that workspace. Honcho needs its own PostgreSQL with pgvector, an LLM provider, and an embedding provider; set EMBEDDING_VECTOR_DIMENSIONS before its first start. WhatEverFi stores only explicitly saved facts in Honcho; conversation summaries stay in WhatEverFi. Bots can forget a saved fact on Honcho v3.2 or later.

MCP servers

Remote MCP servers and installed API / GraphQL connectors default to public HTTPS. The deployment owner can attach one on localhost, the same LAN, or a Docker network. Set MCP_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ENDPOINT=true on the API and worker to allow these for every user. Cloud metadata addresses stay blocked. Leave the flag unset on public installs.

Remote MCP servers that use OAuth normally register WhatEverFi with their provider on the first Connect OAuth. Some providers only accept a client you create in their console. For those, enter the client ID (and secret, for a confidential client) under Advanced when adding the server, and add the Redirect URI shown there (<your web origin>/mcp/oauth/callback) to the client’s allowed redirect URIs. The client is stored encrypted with the server’s other credentials and survives Disconnect; switching to a different client drops the current grant. On first use the client is bound to the authorization server the MCP server pointed to, and WhatEverFi refuses to send it anywhere else afterwards. Replacing the client clears the binding.

Stdio MCP servers can use OAuth too. They do not authorize themselves (the MCP spec has them read credentials from the environment), so WhatEverFi runs the flow for them. They are off unless the API and worker have MCP_STDIO_ENABLED=true and the command is listed in MCP_STDIO_ALLOWED_COMMANDS. A stdio server runs inside the API and worker with their access, so only admins (verified accounts listed in RAKAZO_ADMIN_EMAILS) can add or edit one, in Settings or through an agent import; with no admins listed, nobody can. Bots never add stdio servers. Everyone can still add remote servers, and a stdio server an admin added keeps working for everyone it is available to. When adding the server, enter the OAuth client, its Authorization server (the issuer, for example https://accounts.google.com) and the Scopes, then click Connect OAuth as for a remote server. Some providers issue a refresh token only when asked through extra parameters: for Google, set Authorization parameters to access_type=offline&prompt=consent. Pass the grant to the process through its environment variables:

  • A value can reference {{oauth.access_token}}, {{oauth.refresh_token}}, {{oauth.client_id}}, {{oauth.client_secret}}, {{oauth.expires_at}} (epoch milliseconds), {{oauth.scope}} or {{oauth.token_type}}, alone or inside other text.
  • A variable can be a File instead: its template (often JSON, with the same references) is written to a private temporary directory when the process starts, and the variable receives the file’s path. Use this for packages that read a credentials or token file path.

WhatEverFi refreshes the grant and restarts the process shortly before an access token it passed expires, so a long-running process never keeps a dead token. A process that only receives the refresh token refreshes on its own. Temporary files are removed when the process stops.

A server launched as npx [-y] <package>[@version] (or npx -p <package> <bin>) is not downloaded on every start. WhatEverFi installs the package once, without running its install scripts, with npm install into MCP_PACKAGES_DIR (default DATA_DIR/mcp-packages, shared by the API and worker), then runs its bin directly; npx must still be in MCP_STDIO_ALLOWED_COMMANDS. The install has its own timeout, MCP_STDIO_INSTALL_TIMEOUT_MS (default 180000), separate from the handshake timeout MCP_STDIO_STARTUP_TIMEOUT_MS (default 30000). Pin a version so every start runs the same code; npm settings such as NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY can be set in the server’s environment variables. Any other npx form (local paths, git and tarball URLs, unknown npx flags) is refused. npx is the only supported package launcher: other package managers and runners (npm, pnpm, yarn, bun, bunx, deno, uv, uvx, pipx and the like) are refused even when allowlisted. To run a server from another ecosystem, install it on the host and allowlist its binary. An allowlisted interpreter or shell (node, python, sh) runs any code passed in its arguments, so allowlist it only where that is acceptable. Each server runs as one process per user in each of the API and worker, shared by that user’s bots, and stops after MCP_STDIO_IDLE_MS (default 900000, 15 minutes) without use. When a server fails to start, the reason (including the end of its stderr, with credentials redacted) appears on the server in Settings, and its bots are told it is unavailable instead of silently losing its tools.

Tool discovery keeps at most MCP_MAX_TOOLS tools (default 250) and reads at most MCP_MAX_PAGES pages (default 20) per server, for both remote and stdio MCP servers. Set positive safe integers in .env, for example MCP_MAX_TOOLS=1000 and MCP_MAX_PAGES=100, to change them. Unset, blank or invalid values fall back to the respective default. Discovery stops when either bound is reached or the server has no next page, and remains subject to the existing response-size and timeout limits. Docker deployments need both settings on the API and worker; recreate those containers after changing them.

A run never waits long on one server. It gives each server MCP_DISCOVERY_TIMEOUT_MS (default 20000) to list its tools, then goes on without it; a package still installing finishes in the background and its tools appear on a later turn. After a failure, runs skip that server for 30 seconds, doubling up to 5 minutes while it keeps failing. A successful Test connection or discovery, or a change to the server’s settings, ends the wait at once.

If a server shows its tools in Settings but a bot never uses them, run the diagnostics report. Its Assignment column names any space or owner mismatch that keeps the server’s tools from that bot.

Apps and connectors

Plugins use Composio when COMPOSIO_API_KEY is set. Pipedream is an alternative managed connector provider: set PIPEDREAM_CLIENT_ID, PIPEDREAM_CLIENT_SECRET, PIPEDREAM_PROJECT_ID and PIPEDREAM_ENVIRONMENT (development or production). Set them on the API and worker.

INTEGRATIONS_CATALOG_URL points API connector search at an integrations.sh-compatible catalog, such as a mirror you host. Give the base URL; WhatEverFi appends api/search.

Messaging apps

Optional messaging platforms (iMessage through Sendblue or Photon, Slack, WhatsApp, Telegram, Feishu/Lark) mount when their env credentials are set — see .env.example. The Lark adapter and official SDK load only when configured. Point a Feishu/Lark bot event subscription at /api/v1/messaging/webhook/lark (webhook/HTTP inbound only; do not enable long connection). Personal group linking works on iMessage and Telegram (see the Telegram privacy note below); WhatsApp and Feishu/Lark are direct-only, and Slack channels use workspace installations below. Telegram can run several bots side by side (TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN_<NAME> plus TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET_TOKEN_<NAME>), for example one per space, so the same person can chat with a different WhatEverFi bot through each. Photon works the same way: each extra project (PHOTON_PROJECT_ID_<NAME> plus PHOTON_PROJECT_SECRET_<NAME>, and PHOTON_WEBHOOK_SECRET_<NAME> for webhooks) gives the person a different number, mounted as provider photon-<name>. Photon receives iMessage over an outbound stream from the API, so it works on a server with no public URL; on Photon’s shared lines the person texts first, and group chats are not available.

Each platform turns on when its full set of credentials is present on the API and worker. Webhooks arrive at /api/v1/messaging/webhook/<provider>.

Platform Settings
iMessage and SMS (Sendblue) SENDBLUE_API_KEY_ID, SENDBLUE_API_SECRET, SENDBLUE_SIGNING_SECRET, SENDBLUE_PHONE_NUMBER
WhatsApp Business Cloud WHATSAPP_ACCESS_TOKEN, WHATSAPP_PHONE_NUMBER_ID, WHATSAPP_APP_SECRET, WHATSAPP_VERIFY_TOKEN
Telegram TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET_TOKEN
iMessage (Photon) PHOTON_PROJECT_ID, PHOTON_PROJECT_SECRET; PHOTON_WEBHOOK_SECRET to receive by webhook instead of the stream; more projects as PHOTON_PROJECT_ID_<NAME> plus PHOTON_PROJECT_SECRET_<NAME>
Feishu/Lark LARK_APP_ID, LARK_APP_SECRET, LARK_VERIFICATION_TOKEN; LARK_ENCRYPT_KEY when event encryption is on; LARK_DOMAIN (feishu, the default, or lark)
Microsoft Teams TEAMS_APP_ID, TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD, TEAMS_APP_TENANT_ID (single-tenant, direct messages only)
Slack See below

Telegram is webhook-only: Telegram sends the secret in X-Telegram-Bot-Api-Secret-Token, and the worker never long-polls. An extra bot named <NAME> (letters and digits) uses the provider telegram-<name> and the webhook /api/v1/messaging/webhook/telegram-<name>; see settings with names you choose. Telegram groups use personal group linking, like iMessage: each linked member approves their own bot, and the per-room listening settings belong to Slack team conversations only. In BotFather run /setprivacy on the bot and choose Disable (or make it a group admin), or the bot only receives group messages that mention it. Broadcast channel posts never start runs. For Lark, create a custom app with the Bot capability and subscribe it to im.message.receive_v1.

People link a chat app to their account from Messaging settings. MESSAGING_OPEN_SIGNUP=true instead gives unknown senders their own chat-only accounts, whose runs use the deployment model.

In rooms, a bot decides whether to answer ambient messages with its own model. To use a separate model for that decision, set both TEAM_CHAT_JUDGE_PROVIDER and TEAM_CHAT_JUDGE_MODEL.

Microsoft Teams

Register a single-tenant Azure bot with the Teams channel enabled. Set TEAMS_APP_ID, TEAMS_APP_PASSWORD (the client secret value), and TEAMS_APP_TENANT_ID on the server. Set its messaging endpoint to https://your-domain.example/api/v1/messaging/webhook/teams. Install the Teams app with the bot’s personal scope in your tenant; your administrator may need to allow custom apps. Microsoft JWT verification remains enabled.

Choose teams under Settings → Messaging, then send the link code to the bot in a direct message. Replies and later messages use the linked conversation, including after a server restart. Starting a new DM by user address, Teams channels, and group chats are not supported. No Microsoft Graph history permissions are needed for this direct-message flow.

Slack

For Slack workspace installations, set SLACK_CLIENT_ID, SLACK_CLIENT_SECRET, and SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET on the API and worker. Register the OAuth redirect URL https://app.example.com/api/v1/messaging/install/slack/callback using your public API origin (API_URL). Enable distribution in the Slack app’s Manage Distribution settings so other workspaces can install it. Enable Slack Events API delivery to https://app.example.com/api/v1/messaging/webhook/slack, with app_mention, message.im, message.channels, message.groups, message.mpim, and app_uninstalled. Enable the app’s Messages tab. The install flow requests the message/history, channel/user lookup, file read and write, and reaction-write scopes it uses; reinstall the Slack app after changing scopes. Socket Mode is not used.

In Messaging settings, select Connect on the Slack row. The workspace answers as the first bot in your default space, whichever space is open. Each Slack workspace belongs to one WhatEverFi space and one installation owner; installing it from another space is rejected. To DM that bot, use Link DMs and send the code in a DM to the Slack app. Teammates in the same space can link their own bots the same way. Invite the Slack app to channels and mention it to receive replies there. The bot’s external conversations offer Mentions only, Listen, and room guidance. Workspace setup and personal linking are available on web, desktop and mobile. Mobile opens Slack authorization in the system browser; return to the app when it finishes. Channel listening settings currently live in the web/desktop interface.

Tokens are encrypted with the configured secret store. Workers resolve the installation for every outbound operation, including queued replies; disconnecting an installation stops further delivery and unlinks its personal DMs. Slack’s signed app_uninstalled event also removes the installation. Disconnect removes WhatEverFi’s local credentials; remove the app in Slack to revoke Slack’s installation itself. The installation owner must retain space membership and an active bot. Workspace installations require a workspace-level bot token without Slack token rotation; Enterprise Grid org-wide installs and rotating tokens are rejected explicitly.

The older SLACK_BOT_TOKEN plus SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET configuration still supports a single workspace. OAuth mode takes precedence when configured; existing static Slack identities/conversations must be relinked before using workspace installs. TEAM_CHAT_BOT_ID only selects a channel bot for the static configuration. It does not override workspace installations or personal DMs. Slack tools authorized from the Integrations screen are a separate connection from this messaging surface.

Cloud coding agents

Cloud agents delegate a repository task to a hosted coding agent and track its result in the bot’s chat. They are separate from the bot computer and its in-turn subagents. Web, Electron, and mobile show the same status and pull-request link.

The default is CLOUD_AGENT_PROVIDER=none. Core workflows do not require Cursor or any other hosted coding provider.

Enable Cursor

Configure the API and worker with the same values:

CLOUD_AGENT_PROVIDER=cursor
CLOUD_AGENT_SPACE_ID=example-space-id
CURSOR_API_KEY=replace-with-your-key

The key and explicit Space ID are both required. Use a credential whose connected repositories may be accessed by members of that Space. Each created agent is additionally bound to its initiating user; another user cannot inspect, reply to, or cancel it by supplying an agent ID. The deployment key is never a model tool argument.

The tools are cloud_agent_launch, cloud_agent_status, cloud_agent_reply, and cloud_agent_cancel. All three mutations participate in the existing action-approval rules and auto-review policy. As with other consequential tools, an empty rule set and disabled auto-review permit execution by default.

Launch accepts a prompt, optional repository, images, and openPr. Raw environment variables are intentionally unsupported: passing secrets through model-generated tool arguments would persist them in ordinary history. Configure remote environment secrets directly with the provider.

Recovery

The database stores ownership and pending operations independently of chat cards. The worker and reconciler recover queue failures and interrupted launches. Cursor creates use a stable client agent ID, so retrying an accepted create does not create another remote agent.

Each follow-up tracks its own remote run. When a follow-up response is lost, the worker observes the latest run instead of resending the prompt. Until it can distinguish the new run, status remains pending; it does not claim the older run completed the follow-up. Cancellation likewise remains pending until the remote state confirms it. If a request’s outcome remains unknown indefinitely, inspect the agent on the provider’s site.

Clearing a chat, deleting or archiving its bot, or removing the owner’s Space membership causes pending remote work to be cancelled on the next reconciliation. Clearing a chat does not erase ownership or recreate the removed card. Terminal notifications are deduplicated in the durable record.

The stored credential binding fails closed if the key or provider changes. Cancel or finish active agents before rotating credentials, changing the authorized Space, or disabling the provider. If changed prematurely, restore the previous configuration to reconcile those agents, or stop them directly with the provider. No existing agent is silently routed through a replacement credential.

Offline verification

CLOUD_AGENT_PROVIDER=emulator runs the real Cursor adapter against an in-process Cursor HTTP emulator for development and web E2E. It is not durable across separate processes.

The emulator models run creation, unknown run statuses, archived or expired agents, removed agents and runs, rejected keys, and rate limits without network calls. The conformance suite runs against it, and pnpm test:integration exercises the database lifecycle against the Cursor emulator: lost responses, stale run metadata, queue outages, ownership boundaries, cleared chats, worker restart, overlapping polls, and cancellation races.

Payments

Bots can buy things with their user’s wallet. Each user connects their own wallet, and every purchase asks them to approve it in the wallet provider’s app or page before any card or token exists. Card numbers, security codes and payment tokens go straight to the merchant; they never reach the model, chat history, tool results, or logs.

The default is PAYMENT_WALLET_PROVIDER=none. Core workflows do not require a wallet, and with none configured users see nothing related to payments.

Enable Link

Configure the API and worker with the same values:

PAYMENT_WALLET_PROVIDER=link
# Optional. Defaults to Link's public sign-in client.
PAYMENT_WALLET_CLIENT_ID=

Users then see a Link connect button in Settings. Connecting opens Link’s sign-in page with a code to confirm. Once connected, bots get request_purchase, purchase_status and paid_request. Each request names the amount and reason; the user approves or denies it in Link. A purchase also counts against the user’s spending limit, if they set one, before Link is asked.

Link is available to users in the US and Canada only.

Unknown or blank values fall back to none instead of failing at boot.

How a purchase is paid

  • Card. Approval issues a single-use card. The bot types it into the checkout on the purchase’s own HTTPS origin, in the page or in a known payment provider’s frame on it.
  • Pay token. A Stripe checkout that accepts Link pay tokens says so in the page snapshot, with its merchant account. The bot requests the purchase for that account, and after approval hands the token to the checkout, which then shows the user’s saved Link card. Tokens expire 30 minutes after approval.
  • Paid HTTP requests. paid_request sends an HTTPS request. If the server answers 402 Payment Required with a Machine Payments Protocol challenge for Stripe, the amount comes from the challenge and the user approves it; the bot then sends the request again and it carries the payment. Other payment methods are never paid. The request is stored encrypted until it is sent, it may not carry credentials or cookies, and redirects are reported instead of followed. A payment token is used once; a refused paid request needs a new approval.

Disconnecting

Disconnecting in Settings revokes the connection with the provider. If the provider revokes it first (for example, the user signs out of the connection in Link), purchase tools stop working until the user connects again.

Offline wallet verification

PAYMENT_WALLET_PROVIDER=emulator runs an in-process wallet for development and tests. Sign-in completes immediately; purchases are approved on the next status check, and amounts above 1,000.00 are denied. It fills the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242, issues fake pay tokens, and pays Stripe challenges in 402 responses with a fake token. A shared conformance suite runs against the emulator and against the Link adapter backed by a fake Link API and a fake paid API, without network calls.
